analysis.file_name: 5 was the warning at 6 it gets nasty.pdf
analysis.title: Stuck in a 5% world / 5 was the warning at 6 it gets nasty
key_insights: The 10-year Treasury yield is now above the S&P 500 trailing earnings yield, and the gap versus the dividend yield is around 4 percentage points. Both are near the widest levels since the early 2000s, so bonds now compete with equities for the same capital.

BofA's 5/6/7 framework: at 5% investors historically became agnostic between bonds and equities, at 6% higher yields have been associated with weaker equity returns, and at 7% valuation damage is clearer with multiples compressing materially. The 10-year is already in the first bucket.

Equities have handled the 5-6% yield bucket reasonably well. In months with the 10-year between 5% and 6% and yields rising, the S&P returned an average 0.8%. At 6-7% the average falls to about zero, and above 7% and rising, average monthly returns turn negative.
The reason yields rise matters more near 5%. Growth, productivity and nominal activity are benign drivers. Inflation, sovereign risk or a buyers' strike are far more damaging.

MOVE (rates vol) has surged while equity vol remains comparatively contained. With the 10-year near 5% the discount rate is doing real work, so the speed of repricing the rate path matters more than whether yields are 5.0%, 5.2% or 5.4%.

BofA's normalized valuation framework implies roughly -3% annualized S&P 500 price returns over the next decade, versus about +3% for the equal-weighted index. The S&P trades on 20.4x forward earnings, more expensive than at the start of every tightening cycle since 1983 except 1999/2000.

About 80% of S&P 500 debt is long-term fixed, versus less than 60% in 2007. Net debt/EBITDA is below its long-term average and the effective cost of debt is below 4%. BofA estimates the annualized EPS hit from higher interest expense in 2026-2028 at less than 1% for the S&P 500 ex-financials.

Small caps are more exposed. More than 40% of Russell 2000 debt is short-term or floating rate, and its maturity schedule is more front-loaded than the S&P 500's. A prolonged stay near 5% through the refinancing cycle is the risk.

The S&P has historically produced its weakest average monthly returns during bear flatteners (short rates rising faster than long rates). Real Estate, Utilities and Financials lagged most in those episodes. With the front end driving recent moves, the bear flattener is the curve setup to watch.
S&P 500 balance sheets are well termed out and household leverage has improved versus prior cycles, but US government net interest expense as a share of GDP is at a record high.

tension_points.bull_case: Equities have historically handled the 5-6% yield bucket reasonably well, with a 0.8% average monthly S&P return when yields rise in that range. Corporate balance sheets are well termed out, with about 80% long-term fixed debt, an effective cost below 4%, and a less than 1% annualized EPS hit from interest expense in 2026-2028.
tension_points.bear_case: The S&P trades at 20.4x forward earnings with little valuation cushion, BofA's framework implies -3% annualized S&P price returns over the decade, and rates vol is surging. Small caps with over 40% short-term or floating debt face refinancing pressure, and a bear flattener is historically the weakest regime.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Yields moving above 6%, where average monthly S&P returns fall to about zero, or above 7% and rising, where they turn negative. Also yields driven by inflation, sovereign risk or a buyers' strike rather than growth.

theme_stances.key_argument: With the 10-year above the S&P earnings yield, bonds now compete with equities for capital, though 5% is competition rather than destruction.
theme_stances.evidence: So 5% is competition. It isn't necessarily destruction.
